title: Tamsulosin and Alcohol: Flomax Dizziness, Fainting, and BPH Risks
excerpt: Can you drink on tamsulosin (Flomax)? How the two lower blood pressure together, why fainting at night is the main risk, how alcohol worsens BPH symptoms, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Can you drink on tamsulosin (Flomax)? Why the combo causes dizziness and fainting, how alcohol worsens BPH symptoms, and how to drink more safely.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** most people who take tamsulosin (brand name Flomax) can have a drink or two without a dangerous reaction, and there is no known chemical clash between the drug and alcohol in the liver. The real issue is that both lower your blood pressure, and they do it in ways that stack. Tamsulosin relaxes the muscles in your blood vessel walls; alcohol widens blood vessels and dries you out. Together they make it more likely you'll feel dizzy, light-headed, or even faint when you stand up, especially at night when you get up to use the bathroom. Alcohol can also make the urinary symptoms you're taking tamsulosin for noticeably worse. This guide explains how the two interact, who should be most careful, and the practical habits that keep a night out from ending with a fall.

**The quick rules:** Don't start drinking in the first few days after you begin tamsulosin, raise the dose, or restart it after a break, because that's when the blood-pressure drop is strongest. Keep it to one or two drinks, alternate with water, and eat. Stand up slowly, and sit down to urinate at night if you've been drinking. Don't skip doses to "make room" for alcohol. And if you also take Viagra, Cialis, or a blood pressure pill, talk to your doctor before combining any of them with alcohol.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and prescribing information. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and full medication list. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking on tamsulosin if** you've fainted or nearly fainted on it, you take other blood pressure medicines or erectile dysfunction drugs, you have heart disease, you've had urinary retention before, or you're unsure whether your dose was recently changed. **Get urgent care if** you faint and hit your head, have chest pain or a racing or irregular heartbeat, or can't pass urine at all with a full, painful bladder. In an emergency, call 911.

## How Tamsulosin and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

To understand why the combination causes trouble, it helps to know what each one does on its own.

### What tamsulosin does

Tamsulosin belongs to a group of drugs called **alpha-blockers**. Your body has receptors called alpha-1 receptors on smooth muscle, the involuntary kind of muscle found in your prostate, the neck of your bladder, and the walls of your blood vessels. When adrenaline-type signals hit those receptors, the muscle tightens.

In men with an enlarged prostate (benign prostatic hyperplasia, or BPH), that tightening squeezes the urethra, the tube urine passes through. Tamsulosin blocks the signal, so the muscle around the prostate and bladder neck relaxes. Urine flows more easily, and many men notice a stronger stream, less straining, and fewer trips to the bathroom within a few days to weeks.

Tamsulosin is designed to favor the subtype of alpha-1 receptor found mostly in the prostate (called alpha-1A). That's why it tends to lower blood pressure less than older alpha-blockers like doxazosin (Cardura) and terazosin. But "less" isn't "none." It still has some effect on blood vessels, and the prescribing information warns about **orthostatic hypotension**, which is the medical term for a drop in blood pressure when you stand up. Symptoms include dizziness, light-headedness, blurry vision, and in some people, fainting.

### What alcohol does to blood pressure

Alcohol affects blood pressure in a few ways at once:

- **It widens blood vessels.** That's why your face can flush and you feel warm after a drink. Wider vessels mean lower pressure, at least in the first few hours.
- **It dehydrates you.** Alcohol suppresses a hormone (vasopressin, also called antidiuretic hormone) that normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water. You pee more than you drink, and less fluid in your blood means lower pressure. Our guide on [why alcohol makes you pee](/never-hungover/why-does-alcohol-make-you-pee) explains this in more detail.
- **It dulls your body's quick corrections.** When you stand up, blood pools in your legs, and your nervous system normally tightens your blood vessels and speeds up your heart within seconds to keep blood flowing to your brain. Alcohol can blunt that reflex.
- **It makes you less steady anyway.** Alcohol affects balance and coordination, so a small dizzy spell is more likely to turn into a fall.

### Why they stack

Here's the key point. One of the main ways your body protects you from dizziness when you stand is by tightening blood vessels through those same alpha-1 receptors. Tamsulosin partly blocks that. Alcohol then adds wider vessels, less fluid in the blood, and slower reflexes on top. Each one on its own is often mild. Together they can be enough to drop your blood pressure too far for a few seconds when you get up, and that's when people get dizzy, black out briefly, or fall.

### What doesn't seem to happen

Tamsulosin is broken down in the liver by enzymes called CYP3A4 and CYP2D6. Moderate alcohol isn't known to change those enzymes in a way that meaningfully raises or lowers tamsulosin levels. There's no good evidence of the kind of toxic liver interaction you see with acetaminophen and alcohol. So the concern here is **additive effects** (two things pushing in the same direction), not a chemical reaction between the drug and the drink.

## Flomax and Alcohol: Is There Any Difference?

No. Flomax is the original brand name for tamsulosin, and generic tamsulosin capsules contain the same active ingredient at the same doses, most commonly 0.4 mg once a day (sometimes increased to 0.8 mg). Everything in this article applies equally whether your bottle says Flomax, tamsulosin, or a store brand.

A few related products are worth knowing about:

- **Jalyn** combines tamsulosin with dutasteride, a drug that shrinks the prostate over months. The alcohol advice is the same, because the tamsulosin part is what affects blood pressure.
- **Flomax Relief** is a pharmacy-available version sold in the UK. Same drug, same caution.
- **Other alpha-blockers** such as alfuzosin (Uroxatral), silodosin (Rapaflo), doxazosin, and terazosin work in a similar way. Doxazosin and terazosin are less selective and tend to drop blood pressure more, so the dizziness risk with alcohol is generally higher with those.

## The Biggest Risk: Dizziness and Fainting When You Stand Up

If you take one thing from this article, make it this: the dangerous moment isn't usually while you're sitting with a drink. It's when you stand up afterward.

### The night-time bathroom trip

Picture the common scenario. You've had a few drinks in the evening. Alcohol makes you pee more, so you wake up at 3 a.m. needing the bathroom. You get out of bed quickly, still a bit dehydrated, with tamsulosin in your system and alcohol still in your blood. You walk to the toilet and stand to urinate.

Several things are now working against you at once:

1. **Lying to standing** is the biggest blood-pressure challenge your body faces in a day.
2. **Dehydration from alcohol** means less fluid to work with.
3. **Tamsulosin** has partly blocked the reflex that tightens your blood vessels.
4. **Straining or emptying a full bladder** triggers a nerve reflex that can slow the heart and lower blood pressure further. Doctors call fainting during or right after urination "micturition syncope," and it's especially well known in men who get up at night after drinking.

This is the classic setup for a faint, and falls in bathrooms are dangerous because of hard surfaces, sinks, and tubs.

### When the risk is highest

The prescribing information for tamsulosin notes that dizziness and fainting are most likely at specific times:

- **The first few doses** after you start the medicine.
- **After a dose increase**, for example from 0.4 mg to 0.8 mg.
- **When restarting after a break.** The label advises that if you've missed several days, you should restart at the lowest dose (0.4 mg) rather than jumping back to a higher one, because your body has lost its tolerance to the blood-pressure effect.

Those are the windows when you should be most careful about drinking, or skip alcohol entirely until you know how the medicine affects you.

### How to lower the risk

- **Stand up in stages.** Sit on the edge of the bed for 30 seconds to a minute, then stand, then wait a moment before walking.
- **Sit down to urinate** at night if you've been drinking. It sounds minor, but it removes the most common fall scenario.
- **Keep a light on** or use a night-light on the way to the bathroom.
- **Drink water alongside alcohol** and have a glass before bed to blunt the dehydration.
- **If you feel dizzy, sit or lie down right away.** Don't try to push through it to get back to bed. Most people who faint from low blood pressure would have been fine if they'd sat down a few seconds earlier.

## Alcohol Can Make BPH Symptoms Worse

There's a second reason alcohol and tamsulosin don't sit well together: alcohol works against the reason you're taking the medicine in the first place.

### More urine, more urgency

Tamsulosin helps urine flow out more easily, but it doesn't change how much urine your kidneys make. Alcohol does. A few drinks can noticeably increase how often you need to go, how urgently, and how many times you get up at night. For a man with BPH, that can feel like the medicine has stopped working.

Some drinks are worse than others. Beer adds a lot of fluid volume. Drinks with caffeine (rum and cola, espresso martinis, energy-drink mixers) add a second bladder irritant. Carbonated drinks bother some people's bladders too.

### Night-time urination and sleep

Waking up to pee at night (doctors call it nocturia) is one of the most bothersome BPH symptoms. Alcohol makes it worse in two ways: more urine overnight, and lighter, more broken sleep in the second half of the night as alcohol wears off. More wake-ups also mean more of those risky trips to the bathroom described above.

### Acute urinary retention

This is the one serious BPH complication that alcohol can trigger. **Acute urinary retention** means suddenly being unable to pee at all, even though your bladder is full. It's painful and needs prompt medical care, usually a catheter to drain the bladder.

In men with an enlarged prostate, a known trigger is a large volume of fluid in a short time, especially alcohol, which fills the bladder quickly and can make it harder for the bladder muscle to contract properly. The risk goes up further when alcohol is combined with:

- **Decongestants** like pseudoephedrine (Sudafed), which tighten the muscle around the bladder neck. See our guide to [Sudafed and alcohol](/never-hungover/sudafed-and-alcohol).
- **Sedating antihistamines** like diphenhydramine (Benadryl, many "PM" sleep aids) and the ingredients in night-time cold medicines, which can weaken the bladder's ability to squeeze. Our [NyQuil and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/nyquil-and-alcohol) covers that combination.
- **Holding urine for a long time**, for example on a long drive or at an event without easy bathroom access.
- **Being cold**, which some men find makes retention more likely.

If you have BPH, a binge-style night combined with a cold remedy is exactly the mix to avoid. Tamsulosin lowers the risk of retention but doesn't remove it.

## Tamsulosin, Alcohol, and Erectile Dysfunction Drugs

Many men on tamsulosin also take, or are prescribed, a PDE5 inhibitor such as sildenafil (Viagra) or tadalafil (Cialis). Tadalafil is actually approved to treat BPH symptoms on its own, so some men take it every day.

PDE5 inhibitors also widen blood vessels and lower blood pressure. The prescribing information for these drugs advises caution when they're combined with alpha-blockers, usually by starting at a lower dose and making sure you're stable on one before adding the other. The labels for sildenafil and tadalafil also note that alcohol can add to their blood-pressure-lowering effect.

Put all three together on a date night (tamsulosin, a PDE5 inhibitor, and several drinks) and you have three things pushing your blood pressure down at once. That doesn't mean it's off-limits for everyone, but it's the combination most worth discussing with your doctor before you try it. Keep alcohol light, stay hydrated, and be very careful about standing up quickly. Our guides on [Viagra and alcohol](/never-hungover/viagra-and-alcohol) and [Cialis and alcohol](/never-hungover/cialis-and-alcohol) go into those drugs in more depth.

## Other Medicines That Add to the Risk

Because the main concern is blood pressure, any other medicine that lowers it can make the tamsulosin-plus-alcohol combination more noticeable. Common ones include:

- **Blood pressure pills**, such as ACE inhibitors (lisinopril), beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, and diuretics ("water pills"). See our [lisinopril and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/lisinopril-and-alcohol) and our broader [alcohol and blood pressure guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-hypertension-blood-pressure-management-2025).
- **Other alpha-blockers.** Taking two alpha-blockers together is generally not recommended at all.
- **Nitrates** for chest pain, especially when combined with ED drugs.
- **Sedating medicines** such as sleeping pills, some antidepressants, and opioid painkillers, which add drowsiness and fall risk.

Tamsulosin's levels can also be raised by strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as the antifungal ketoconazole, and the label advises against using it with them. That isn't an alcohol issue, but it's another reason to give your pharmacist your full medication list.

For a wider look at how alcohol interacts with everyday prescriptions, see our [alcohol and medications guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-medications).

## Tamsulosin for Kidney Stones: What About Alcohol?

Doctors often prescribe tamsulosin off-label (meaning for a use not on the official label) to help kidney stones pass. By relaxing the muscle in the ureter, the tube from the kidney to the bladder, it can make it easier for a small stone to move through. This is why some women and younger men end up on tamsulosin for a few weeks.

If that's why you're taking it, alcohol has a few extra downsides:

- **Hydration is part of the treatment.** You're usually told to drink plenty of fluid to help flush the stone. Alcohol is a poor substitute for water because it makes you lose fluid.
- **You may also be taking painkillers.** Stone pain is often treated with NSAIDs like ibuprofen or ketorolac, and sometimes with opioids. Alcohol adds stomach and kidney strain with NSAIDs and dangerous sedation with opioids.
- **You're likely new to tamsulosin.** A short course means you're in the first-dose window when blood-pressure drops are most common.

Most doctors would suggest skipping alcohol while you're actively passing a stone. If you're curious about the link between drinking and stones in general, see [does alcohol cause kidney stones](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-cause-kidney-stones).

## Should You Skip Your Dose If You're Planning to Drink?

It's a common instinct, but generally no. Here's why:

- **Skipping doses can make things worse, not better.** If you miss several days and then restart, you lose your tolerance to the blood-pressure effect and you're back in the higher-risk first-dose window. The label specifically advises restarting at 0.4 mg after a gap of several days.
- **One skipped dose doesn't clear the drug quickly.** Tamsulosin works over a full day, and the effect doesn't switch off the moment you skip a capsule.
- **Your BPH symptoms may come back** that night, right when alcohol is also increasing your urine output.

The better approach is to keep taking it as prescribed and change how you drink. If you're thinking about stopping or changing your dose for any reason, talk to your doctor first.

### What about timing?

Tamsulosin's label advises taking it about 30 minutes after the same meal each day. Many people take it after dinner, which happens to be when evening drinking starts. Some doctors suggest the evening timing on purpose, because any dizziness peaks while you're asleep. Don't change your schedule on your own to work around a night out. If you're regularly drinking around the time you take your dose, ask your doctor or pharmacist whether a different time would suit you better.

Also, swallow the capsules whole. Crushing, chewing, or opening them changes how the drug is released and can cause a bigger blood-pressure drop.

## How Much Alcohol Is Reasonable on Tamsulosin?

There's no official safe number specific to tamsulosin, and anyone who gives you an exact figure is guessing. What can be said with reasonable confidence:

| Situation | General guidance |
|---|---|
| First days on tamsulosin, after a dose increase, or after restarting | Best to avoid alcohol until you know how you react. |
| Stable on 0.4 mg, no dizziness, no other BP drugs | Light drinking (one or two drinks) is usually tolerated. Hydrate and stand up slowly. |
| Also taking an ED drug, BP pills, or other alpha-blockers | Ask your doctor first. Keep alcohol minimal. |
| History of fainting, falls, or urinary retention | Talk to your doctor before drinking at all. |
| Older adults (especially 65+) | Falls carry more risk. Be extra cautious, particularly at night. |
| Passing a kidney stone | Most doctors suggest skipping alcohol until it's passed. |

A "standard drink" in the US is roughly one 12-ounce beer, one 5-ounce glass of wine, or one 1.5-ounce shot of spirits. Strong craft beers and generous wine pours can count as two.

## Practical Tips for Drinking Safely on Tamsulosin

If you've talked it over with your doctor and decided to drink, these habits make the biggest difference:

1. **Eat before and while drinking.** Food slows alcohol absorption and softens the blood-pressure dip.
2. **Pace yourself.** Your body processes roughly one standard drink per hour, though that varies a lot between people.
3. **Alternate with water.** One glass of water per drink helps with dehydration and dilutes the effect on your bladder.
4. **Choose lower-volume drinks.** A glass of wine or a single spirit with a non-caffeinated mixer means less fluid for your bladder than several pints of beer.
5. **Stop drinking a couple of hours before bed** and empty your bladder before you lie down.
6. **Get up slowly**, especially at night and first thing in the morning.
7. **Sit down to pee** at night after drinking.
8. **Skip cold medicines and sleep aids** the same night, especially anything with pseudoephedrine or diphenhydramine.
9. **Don't drive** if you feel even slightly dizzy. Both alcohol and tamsulosin can affect alertness and reaction time.

## The Morning After: Hangovers on Tamsulosin

A hangover adds its own dehydration on top of tamsulosin's effect on blood pressure, so the morning after drinking is another time to be careful about standing up quickly. If you feel light-headed:

- **Drink water or an electrolyte drink first**, before getting up and moving around much. Our guide to [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking) covers what actually helps.
- **Eat something salty** if you can, which helps your body hold onto fluid.
- **Be careful with painkillers.** Ibuprofen and other NSAIDs can strain the kidneys when you're dehydrated, and they can also slightly blunt the effect of some blood pressure drugs. Acetaminophen has its own alcohol cautions for the liver.
- **Avoid "hangover" combination products** that contain antihistamines or decongestants, for the urinary-retention reasons above.

A pounding heart, dizziness that doesn't settle when you sit, or feeling faint repeatedly isn't a normal hangover. If you notice your heart racing, see our guide on [heart racing after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking), and call your doctor if it keeps happening.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help

**Call your doctor soon if:**

- You get dizzy or light-headed often when standing, with or without alcohol.
- You nearly fainted or fainted once without injury.
- Your urinary symptoms are getting worse despite the medicine.
- You notice blurred vision, unusual tiredness, or swelling.

**Get urgent medical care (or call 911) if:**

- You faint and hit your head, or can't remember how you fell.
- You have chest pain, shortness of breath, or a very fast or irregular heartbeat.
- **You can't urinate at all** and your lower belly is swollen and painful. This is acute urinary retention and needs prompt treatment.
- You have an erection that lasts more than four hours (a rare but recognized side effect of alpha-blockers called priapism).
- You notice signs of a serious allergic reaction such as swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or trouble breathing.

**Planning eye surgery?** If you're scheduled for cataract or glaucoma surgery, tell your eye surgeon you take (or have ever taken) tamsulosin. It's linked to a condition called floppy iris syndrome that the surgeon needs to plan for. This has nothing to do with alcohol, but it's one of the most important tamsulosin safety points and it's often missed.

## Can DHM or Other Hangover Supplements Help?

Some people who drink occasionally use supplements to feel better the next day. Here's an honest look at where they fit for someone on tamsulosin.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data. There are no studies looking specifically at DHM and tamsulosin, so there's no good evidence either way about whether they interact. DHM does **not** protect you from the blood-pressure drop that is the main tamsulosin-and-alcohol concern, and it doesn't make it safe to drink more. If you want to try it, show the label to your pharmacist first, since they can check it against your full medication list. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what's known about DHM and common prescriptions.

If you get the all-clear, well-reviewed options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

**Electrolyte drinks** are a more direct help for the specific problem here. Replacing the fluid and salt alcohol pulls out can ease the dehydration that makes tamsulosin-related dizziness worse. If you have heart or kidney disease or are on a low-salt diet, check with your doctor first.

The most effective step is still the simplest one: drink less, drink slower, and drink water in between.

## The Bottom Line

- There's no known toxic chemical interaction between tamsulosin (Flomax) and alcohol, but **both lower blood pressure, and the effects add up**.
- The main danger is **dizziness, fainting, and falls when you stand up**, especially getting up at night to urinate after drinking.
- Risk is highest in the **first few days on tamsulosin, after a dose increase, or after restarting** following a break.
- Alcohol can **worsen BPH symptoms** and, especially with decongestants or sedating antihistamines, can trigger **acute urinary retention**.
- Combining tamsulosin with **Viagra, Cialis, or blood pressure pills** plus alcohol adds more risk. Ask your doctor first.
- If you drink, keep it light, eat, hydrate, stand up slowly, sit to pee at night, and don't skip doses to make room for alcohol.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking tamsulosin?**

Many people on a stable dose of tamsulosin can have a drink or two without serious problems, but the combination isn't risk-free. Both tamsulosin and alcohol lower blood pressure, so together they make dizziness and fainting more likely, especially when you stand up. Avoid alcohol in the first few days of treatment, after a dose increase, or after restarting. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist about your own situation, especially if you take other blood pressure or erectile dysfunction medicines.

**Is it safe to drink alcohol with Flomax?**

Flomax is the brand name for tamsulosin, so the advice is the same. There's no known toxic reaction between Flomax and alcohol, but they both lower blood pressure. The combination can cause light-headedness, fainting, and falls, most often when getting up quickly or at night. Keep alcohol light, stay hydrated, stand up slowly, and check with your doctor before drinking if you've had dizzy spells on the medicine.

**Why does tamsulosin make me dizzy when I drink?**

Tamsulosin partly blocks alpha-1 receptors that help tighten your blood vessels when you stand up. Alcohol widens blood vessels, dehydrates you, and dulls your body's quick blood-pressure corrections. Together they can let your blood pressure drop too far for a few seconds when you change position, which causes dizziness or a brief blackout. Sitting or lying down right away usually helps. If it happens often, tell your doctor.

**Can alcohol make BPH or prostate symptoms worse?**

Yes. Alcohol makes your kidneys produce more urine, which means more frequent and urgent trips to the bathroom and more waking up at night. Caffeinated and carbonated mixers can irritate the bladder further. In men with an enlarged prostate, heavy drinking, especially combined with decongestants or sedating antihistamines, can trigger acute urinary retention, a sudden inability to urinate that needs prompt medical care.

**Should I skip my tamsulosin dose if I'm going to drink?**

Generally no. Skipping doses doesn't quickly remove the drug's effect, your urinary symptoms may return, and if you miss several days, restarting puts you back in the higher-risk window for dizziness and fainting. The tamsulosin label advises restarting at the lowest dose after a gap of several days. Keep taking it as prescribed and drink less instead, and talk to your doctor before changing your dose or schedule.

**Can I take tamsulosin and Cialis or Viagra and drink alcohol?**

This combination needs extra care, because tamsulosin, PDE5 inhibitors like sildenafil and tadalafil, and alcohol all lower blood pressure. The prescribing information for these drugs advises caution when combining them with alpha-blockers, and alcohol adds to the effect. Talk to your doctor before combining them. If you've been cleared, keep alcohol to a minimum, stay hydrated, and stand up slowly.

**Can I drink alcohol while taking tamsulosin for kidney stones?**

Most doctors suggest avoiding alcohol while you're passing a kidney stone. Drinking plenty of water is part of the treatment, and alcohol makes you lose fluid instead. You're also likely new to tamsulosin, which is when blood-pressure drops are most common, and you may be taking painkillers that don't mix well with alcohol. Wait until the stone has passed and you've finished the course.

**How long after taking tamsulosin can I drink alcohol?**

There's no official waiting period, because tamsulosin is taken once a day and works around the clock. Timing your drink a few hours after the capsule won't avoid the interaction. What matters more is being on a stable dose, keeping alcohol light, eating, staying hydrated, and being careful when you stand up. If you regularly drink around the time you take your dose, ask your pharmacist whether a different time would work better.

**Does DHM interact with tamsulosin?**

There are no studies looking at DHM and tamsulosin together, so there's no good evidence either way about an interaction. DHM does not protect against the blood-pressure drop that is the main concern with tamsulosin and alcohol, and it doesn't make it safe to drink more. If you want to try a DHM supplement, show the label to your pharmacist first so they can check it against your full medication list.

If you want to try a DHM supplement, show the label to your pharmacist first so they can check it against your full medication list.
